name: Pneumonia
tagline: Top killer of under-5s and over-65s.

urgent.heading: Urgent — see a clinic now
urgent.primary_message: Pneumonia in young children and the elderly can become deadly within hours. Difficulty breathing, blue lips, severe weakness — go to hospital.
red_flags: Difficulty breathing or breathing very fast
Cannot keep fluids down — vomiting everything
Chest pain that worsens with breathing
Confusion or unusual drowsiness, especially in elderly
In a child under 5: chest sucking in between ribs, refusal to feed, listlessness
Cough producing rust-coloured, green, or blood-streaked mucus

what_is_it.heading: Pneumonia in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Pneumonia is an infection of the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs. The sacs fill with fluid or pus, making it hard to breathe and starving the body of oxygen.
paragraphs: Most pneumonia is caused by bacteria — Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common. Viruses and fungi can also cause it. The infection often follows a cold or flu, when the immune system is weakened.

Healthy adults usually recover well with antibiotics or supportive care. The danger is concentrated in three groups: children under 5, adults over 65, and people with chronic conditions or HIV. In these groups, pneumonia is one of South Africa's top killers.

items.headline: Top killer
items.body: Pneumonia is among the leading causes of death in SA children under 5 and adults over 65.

items.headline: Vaccine-preventable
items.body: Pneumococcal vaccine — free for children, recommended for over-65s and chronic illness. Cuts the most common type significantly.

items.headline: Curable
items.body: Bacterial pneumonia responds to antibiotics within days. Treatment must be completed in full — never stop early.

items.headline: Often follows flu
items.body: Many pneumonias start as a viral chest infection that becomes bacterial. This is why a flu that gets worse after 5–7 days needs medical assessment.

pull_quote.text: Pneumonia in a small child can go from a cough to critical in 24 hours. If a child is breathing fast, refusing to feed, or has chest indrawing — do not wait for morning. Go now.

signs.heading: What pneumonia looks like
signs.lede: Pneumonia symptoms range from mild walking-pneumonia to severe and life-threatening. Children and elderly often show atypical signs.

items.title: Classic symptoms
items.description: Cough (often with thick green, yellow, or rust-coloured mucus), fever and chills, difficulty breathing, chest pain that worsens with breathing.

items.title: Elderly may not have fever
items.description: Older adults often present with confusion, weakness, falls, or worsening of underlying conditions — without obvious fever or cough.

items.title: Children
items.description: Fast breathing, chest indrawing (skin pulling in between or below ribs with each breath), refusing to feed, grunting, blue lips — these need immediate attention.

spreads.heading: How pneumonia spreads
yes: Coughs and sneezes spreading bacteria or viruses from infected people
Close contact in households, day care, or care homes
Aspiration of food, drink, or stomach contents into the lungs (in older or weakened adults)
Following another respiratory infection like flu or COVID

prevention.heading: How to lower the risk
prevention.lede: Most pneumonia in young children, the elderly, and chronically ill people is preventable with vaccines, hand washing, and treating respiratory infections early.

items.title: Pneumococcal vaccine
items.description: Free for children at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 months. Recommended for adults over 65 and chronic illness — ask at clinic.

items.title: Annual flu vaccine
items.description: Flu often leads to pneumonia. Preventing flu prevents many secondary pneumonias. Free for high-risk groups.

items.title: Don't smoke
items.description: Smoking damages the lungs' defences and is a major risk factor for pneumonia. Quitting reduces risk within months.

items.title: Hand hygiene
items.description: Wash hands often, especially around small children, elderly relatives, or anyone with chronic illness.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.fact: Pneumonia can strike at any age. Children, young people, athletes — all get it. For most it is treatable — but it must be treated.

items.myth: Cough remedies and steam are enough to cure pneumonia.
items.fact: Bacterial pneumonia needs antibiotics. Steam and home remedies can ease symptoms but won't clear the infection. See a doctor.

items.myth: If I feel better after a few days, I can stop my antibiotics.
items.fact: Stopping antibiotics early lets some bacteria survive, become resistant, and bring the infection back — sometimes worse. Complete the full course.

items.myth: Pneumonia is always the same — treat it once and you're done.
items.fact: Different germs cause different pneumonias, and the right antibiotic differs. That's why a doctor — not self-treatment — should choose the treatment.

items.title: See a clinic for any persistent chest infection
items.description: A cough that does not improve after 7 days, especially with fever, chest pain, or breathing difficulty, needs medical assessment.

items.title: If diagnosed — take the full antibiotic course
items.description: Most bacterial pneumonia is treated with 5–7 days of antibiotics. Take every dose even if you feel better — stopping early can let infection rebound.

items.title: Rest fully until recovered
items.description: Pneumonia exhausts the body. Plan for at least a week off work or school. Pushing through delays recovery and risks complications.

items.title: Watch for danger signs
items.description: Fast or laboured breathing, blue lips, confusion, chest pain, inability to keep fluids down — go to hospital immediately.

items.title: Get vaccines after recovery
items.description: Once recovered, ask your clinic about pneumococcal and flu vaccines if you have not had them. Prevents the next episode.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Mild pneumonia can be treated at home with antibiotics from a clinic. Severe pneumonia is a hospital emergency.
